stem: A 20-month-old is being reviewed for recurrent wheeze; which developmental change after infancy best explains why wheeze beyond 12 months begins to resemble asthma or viral-induced wheeze more than earlier infant pathology?

options.text: Airway diameter and smooth muscle development increase after 12 months
Chest tightness becomes the most reliable symptom in all toddlers
Spirometry becomes universally reproducible in all children after 12 months
Bacterial pneumonia becomes the usual cause of wheeze after 12 months
Children older than 12 months should always be diagnosed with asthma if they wheeze

explanation: Airway diameter and smooth muscle development increase after 12 months. This developmental change means recurrent wheeze in toddlers is more likely to resemble asthma or viral-induced wheeze than the pathology seen in younger infants.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

optionExplanations.A: Correct because increasing airway diameter and smooth muscle development after 12 months helps explain why wheeze starts to resemble asthma or viral-induced wheeze.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because chest tightness is not the developmental change that explains the shift in wheeze after infancy.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because spirometry is not universally reproducible in all children after 12 months.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because bacterial pneumonia is not the usual developmental explanation for wheeze after 12 months.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because wheeze after 12 months does not always mean asthma; the diagnosis still depends on the broader clinical picture.
